scores.justification: The tutor misreads the scenario from the start, treating 'each connected one at a time' as a SERIES circuit and concluding 'R2 will have a higher voltage drop because it has more resistance' (turn 1). This actively validates a wrong frame and never identifies the voltage/current conflation. It diagnoses the student as needing series-circuit voltage division, which is the wrong problem and the wrong misconception.

Turn 1 is a full structured lecture with the complete worked solution, not Socratic scaffolding. From turn 3 onward the exchange degenerates into repeated near-identical recaps and mutual congratulation ('that's spot on!'), then the tutor launches its own off-topic complex-circuit and Bernoulli problems. There is essentially no interactive structure that hands reasoning to the student.

The very first tutor turn computes everything and rewrites the student's answer for them, even providing a finished 'correctly rephrased' answer. It immediately gives the full answer and explanation, the rubric's definition of a 0.

Concepts are presented as series-circuit rules ('higher resistance means higher voltage drop', 'current is the same in series') applied to a misframed problem. No transferable cause/effect model for voltage vs current is built, and the framing it does build is wrong for the stated single-resistor scenario.

On the water-tower transfer the tutor gives an outright WRONG answer via misapplied Bernoulli/continuity, concluding 'the pipe with the smaller inner diameter (higher velocity) will carry a greater flow rate.' The student echoes this incorrect conclusion. The transfer is failed completely.

Multiple incorrect-physics moves: misreads 'one at a time' as a series circuit and asserts R2 has the higher voltage drop, and on transfer claims the narrower/smaller-diameter pipe carries greater flow rate. These reinforce the very voltage/current (pressure/flow) conflation under test and teach wrong physics. Clear 0.
